fixes.explanation: That's what the LORD tells David: "It is because of the blood shed by Saul and his family, because he killed the Gibeonites." Saul was Israel's king before David (1 Samuel 11:15). David sought the face of the LORD, and the LORD gave him the cause. When you're stuck, friend, asking the One who knows beats staring at the empty cookie jar.

The LORD never mentions idols here. He gives one cause: the blood shed by Saul and his family, because Saul killed the Gibeonites, a people who were not Israelites. David sought the face of the LORD, and that's the answer he got. I think a clear answer like that saves a lot of guessing.

Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjamite, did lead a revolt against David (2 Samuel 20:1-2), but that's not what the LORD points to here. He says the famine is "…because of the blood shed by Saul and his family, because he killed the Gibeonites." Saul was Israel's king before David (1 Samuel 11:15). Two big troubles, friend, but only one is the answer to this question.

Careful here, friend, because the text says the opposite. Israel had taken an oath concerning the Gibeonites, but "…in his zeal for Israel and Judah, Saul had sought to kill them." So Saul, Israel's king before David (1 Samuel 11:15), did not keep it. That's why the famine story starts where it does.

David asks, "What shall I do for you? How can I make amends so that you may bless the inheritance of the LORD?" Notice he asks first and doesn't just announce a plan. Then the Gibeonites get to answer him. Good leaders, friend, ask before they act.

David does agree. After the Gibeonites make their request, the king says, "I will give them to you…" He had told them, "Whatever you ask, I will do for you…" and now he says yes to their request. It's a heavy moment, friend.

The text says the king spared him "…because of the oath before the LORD between David and Jonathan son of Saul." Jonathan was Saul's son and David's close friend. Back then Jonathan told David, "…we have sworn friendship with each other in the name of the LORD" (1 Samuel 20:42). David remembered the oath, and that's the reason the text gives.

That's not what the text says. Rizpah, Saul's concubine, kept away "…the birds of the air…" by day and "…the beasts of the field…" by night. Two of the seven were her own sons. She spread sackcloth for herself on a rock.

That's right. The text says she kept watch "From the beginning of the harvest until the rain from heaven poured down on the bodies…" Until then, she did not allow the birds or the beasts to rest on them. The rain is where the text marks the end of her watch.

The text says her watch did end at a certain point. It says she kept it "From the beginning of the harvest until the rain from heaven poured down on the bodies…" So the rain is what the text gives as the end of her watch.

The text says David "…went and took the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan…" from the men of Jabesh-gilead. Saul was Israel's king before David (1 Samuel 11:15), and Jonathan was Saul's son. The text tells us this happened when David was told what Rizpah had done.

The text says the bones were buried "…in the tomb of Saul’s father Kish." Saul and Jonathan were laid in the family tomb in Zela, in the land of Benjamin. A family tomb is a quiet, settled place to rest.
